root_cause.text: The `tap_ioctl()` function in `drivers/net/tap.c` fails to initialize the on-stack `struct sockaddr_storage ss` variable, leading to a kernel stack information leak when copying the structure to userspace because `netif_get_mac_address()` only partially populates it.
root_cause.evidence: The patch diff shows that `struct sockaddr_storage ss;` is changed to `struct sockaddr_storage ss = {};` to initialize it at declaration. The CVE description states that "tap_ioctl() copies 16 bytes of an uninitialised on-stack struct sockaddr_storage to userspace via ifr_hwaddr, but netif_get_mac_address() only writes sa_family and dev->addr_len (6 for Ethernet) bytes, leaving sa_data[6..13] uninitialised."

    net: core: Convert dev_set_mac_address_user() to use struct sockaddr_storage
    
    Convert callers of dev_set_mac_address_user() to use struct

    Signed-off-by: Kees Cook <kees@kernel.org>
    Acked-by: Gustavo A. R. Silva <gustavoars@kernel.org>

bic_trace_step.reason: The function `tap_ioctl` declares `struct sockaddr_storage ss;` on the stack without initialization. In the `SIOCGIFHWADDR` case, `dev_get_mac_address` is called with `&ss`, which only partially populates the structure (writing the family and the MAC address up to `dev->addr_len`, typically 6 bytes for Ethernet). Then, `copy_to_user` copies `sizeof(ifr->ifr_hwaddr)` (16 bytes) from `ss` to userspace, leaking the uninitialized bytes of the stack variable `ss` to userspace. The fix of initializing `ss` (e.g., `struct sockaddr_storage ss = {};`) is not present in this commit.
